claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by rapid formation and sustained stability of a Cr-enriched passive oxide layer.
Minor alloying elements such as Mo further stabilize the Cr-enriched passive layer.
The passive layer minimizes ion transport and metal dissolution under aggressive chemical and radiation conditions.
Standard thermomechanical processing can produce a uniform stainless-steel microstructure free of significant inclusions.
The relevant passive film is continuous, nanocrystalline, and rich in Cr2O3.
The Cr2O3-rich passive film forms within minutes of exposure.
Mo suppresses localized breakdown and pitting of the passive film.
Chromium at the steel surface rapidly oxidizes in aggressive aqueous environments to form a dense Cr2O3 layer.
The dense Cr2O3 layer decreases ionic and electronic transport.
Reduced ionic and electronic transport mitigates further oxidation and metal dissolution.
Mo additions enhance passive-film integrity and facilitate self-healing after mechanical or radiolytic damage.
Radiation can generate defects in the passive film.
The composition and close adherence of the passive film allow it to retain barrier properties under radiation.
Higher chloride concentrations and simulated radiation will produce thicker and more Cr2O3-enriched passive films than the stated low-chloride, room-temperature, non-irradiated baseline.
Films formed under higher chloride concentrations and simulated radiation will exhibit lower corrosion current densities and higher impedance values than the stated baseline.
Increasing Cr and Mo alloying levels will correlate with improved film stability and less pitting or localized breakdown.
Steels with lower Cr content or without Mo will undergo faster passive-film breakdown and higher corrosion rates.
Low-alloy or lower-Cr steels develop less uniform or thinner passive films and show higher corrosion rates and pitting incidence under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies to aqueous chemical-processing and light-water-reactor environments up to approximately 120°C and moderate radiation fluxes.
The mechanism may not apply above 300°C, under supercritical conditions, or in steels with heterogeneous microstructures or significant inclusion content.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined inconsistently. The conditions field uses the same steel in low-chloride, room-temperature, non-irradiated conditions, whereas the baseline and falsification fields use low-alloy or lower-Cr steels under identical aggressive conditions. These comparisons alter different variables and cannot serve as a single baseline.
